strengths: The paper targets an important problem: learning collective variables that capture slow molecular dynamics for enhanced sampling, rather than only separating metastable states.
The proposed TLC objective is intuitively appealing as a bottlenecked time-lagged conditional generative model, and the connection to TAE/VDE and flow matching is reasonably motivated.
The manuscript evaluates the learned CVs in two downstream enhanced-sampling settings, SMD and OPES, rather than relying only on static classification or visualization.
The figures and appendices provide useful qualitative diagnostics, including Ramachandran plots, sensitivity analysis, ablations, transition paths, and free-energy convergence curves.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is far too narrow for a top-tier AI venue: all main results are on Alanine Dipeptide, a small benchmark with known optimal dihedral CVs. There is no evidence that the method scales to larger molecules, multiple slow modes, solvent effects beyond this toy setting, or realistic drug/material systems.

The main comparisons are confounded by input representation choices. TLC benefits from RMSD-aligned Cartesian coordinates, while several baselines use heavy-atom distances; the ablation shows representation choice has a very large effect, so the reported gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed time-lagged generative objective.

The method relies on alignment to a reference C5 metastable configuration, which injects domain/state knowledge and weakens claims of automated CV discovery. The generality of this reference-state alignment is not demonstrated.

The SMD evaluation has fairness and interpretability issues: the force constant is tuned per method, the selection criterion is based on a maximum-energy threshold, transition energy is averaged only over successful trajectories, and the energy definition/offset is unclear. The extremely large energy gap between TLC and baselines therefore needs much stronger validation.

The OPES results do not strongly support superiority. Most methods recover similar free-energy differences within the stated tolerance, TLC has nontrivial variance, and some qualitative claims are internally awkward, e.g. VDE is said to show only one basin while its free-energy difference is close to reference.

Technical and reproducibility details are incomplete or unclear: the TLC generative architecture, optimizer, training schedule, lambda choice, dataset size, code release, and hyperparameter tuning protocol are underspecified; Appendix C appears to contain an unfinished code-availability sentence and omits VDE from the model-configuration table.

The novelty over time-lagged autoencoders, VDE, and predictive bottleneck methods is incremental unless the generative modeling component is shown to matter beyond this benchmark. The paper does not evaluate generation quality or convincingly isolate why conditional flow matching yields better CVs.

Several mathematical descriptions are imprecise, including the use of 'conditional Boltzmann distribution' for a time-lagged transition-like conditional, confusing flow-time versus MD-time notation in the TLC loss, and ambiguous notation in the autocorrelation loss.
